name: Learned extraction: Web2Text (Vogels, Ganea & Eickhoff, ECIR 2018, arXiv:1801.02607), GROWN+UP (Yeoh & Wang, CIKM 2022, arXiv:2208.02252), and GoldMiner (Endredy & Novak, Polibits 48, 2013), plus adjacent learned boilerplate-removal work encountered while researching them: Dragnet (Peters & Lecocq 2013), CETD/CETD-DS (Weninger, Hsu & Han 2010), and BoilerNet (Leonhardt, Anand & Khosla, arXiv:2004.14294). All three primary items solve 'boilerplate removal' (label DOM text as main content vs template/noise), not HTML->Markdown transduction -- this distinguishes them sharply from the Reader-LM item in this set, which generates a full serialization rather than classifying existing spans.
kind: Three distinct research results, closer in kind to each other than to Reader-LM: Web2Text and GROWN+UP are trained classifiers (CNN+HMM and GNN respectively) with public code; GoldMiner is a statistical pattern-mining algorithm layered on top of an existing rule-based extractor (jusText), not a gradient-trained model at all, despite sharing the 'learned extraction' label with the other two in casual usage. All three are academic research results with reference implementations, not commercial services.
maturity: All three are dated, single-paper results with no evidence of continued maintenance found in this research. Web2Text (2018) and GoldMiner (2013) predate the JS-heavy, shadow-DOM web this project targets by 6-13 years; GROWN+UP (2022) is the most recent and the only one evaluated against then-contemporary competitors (BoilerNet, Dragnet, its own re-implementations), but its own GitHub repository shows a single release cycle with no indication of ongoing development past the paper. None has a hosted API, a maintained package on PyPI/npm, or a commercial wrapper (contrast Reader-LM's Jina-hosted deployment) -- these are archive-code research artifacts, not production tools, and should be read as datapoints about what learned extraction can achieve, not as adoptable dependencies.
license: Three different licenses, none blocking for research reference. Web2Text: MIT (github.com/dalab/web2text, confirmed via GitHub API license endpoint). GROWN+UP: Apache-2.0 (github.com/benyeoh/grownup, confirmed via GitHub API license endpoint). GoldMiner: no LICENSE file detected in the GitHub mirror (github.com/endredy/GoldMiner; the GitHub API license endpoint returned 404 Not Found), which under GitHub's own terms defaults to all-rights-reserved absent an explicit grant -- [uncertain] whether the paper's text or repository README states different terms elsewhere; this should be verified before using GoldMiner's code directly rather than only its published algorithm description.
keeps_and_discards: All three are binary classifiers or classifier-equivalents over existing text, not generators -- this is the single most important structural fact distinguishing every item in this file from Reader-LM. Web2Text and GROWN+UP each assign a content/boilerplate label to every DOM-leaf text block (Web2Text) or DOM-tag node (GROWN+UP) and keep only the ones labeled content; nothing is invented, so the confabulation failure mode documented for Reader-LM is structurally impossible here -- the worst these systems can do is mislabel, not fabricate. GoldMiner is a step removed again: it does not itself classify content, it learns a per-(sub)domain HTML boundary (a start/end tag pattern) from a sample of pages, trims every page in that domain to the region between those tags, and then hands the trimmed HTML to jusText (a rule-based paragraph classifier) for the actual keep/discard decision -- GoldMiner's own contribution is narrowing jusText's input, not making the final call. All three inherit whatever the ground-truth alignment or labeling procedure defined as 'content' during training/learning, which for CleanEval-derived labels means editorial judgment from 2007 annotators about what counts as an article's main text.
structure_preserved: Varies by design intent, and the variation is informative. Web2Text deliberately works at DOM-LEAF (#text node) granularity after 'collapsing' single-child parent chains (their Collapsed DOM / CDOM), and encodes hierarchy only indirectly through 128 per-block features (parent/grandparent/root statistics) and 25 edge features (tree distance between neighboring blocks, capped at 'greater than 4'); the output is a flat sequence of kept text blocks with no explicit structural markup carried forward -- nesting, tables, and lists are not reconstructed, only detected as being present via tag-type one-hot features. GROWN+UP is structurally the richest of the three: it represents the entire DOM as a directed graph with three edge types (node-to-parent, node-to-child, node-to-self) and per-node features including tag type, font weight/style/size, child count and child index, so structural relationships are preserved as input to the model far more completely than Web2Text's tree-distance-only edge features -- but the OUTPUT is still a per-node binary label, so this richer structural awareness feeds classification accuracy, not a structured serialization; GROWN+UP does not emit a table, list, or nesting-aware output format any more than Web2Text does. GoldMiner preserves whatever structure survives its two-stage crop-then-jusText pipeline, which is to say: whatever jusText's own paragraph/block splitting produces, which is a flat block sequence like the other two, but only within a domain-learned tag boundary. None of the three produces Markdown, JSON, or any structured export -- all three stop at 'this block is content', which is a strictly narrower deliverable than every serializer item elsewhere in this project's list.
interactive_elements: Not addressed by any of the three, and structurally out of scope for all: Web2Text's preprocessing explicitly REMOVES nodes with no extractable content including , ,
interactive_state_fidelity: Not applicable -- none of the three retains any element that would carry such state (see interactive_elements). This is a clean 'not addressed' rather than a partial/degraded case: the entire category of disabled/checked/selected/expanded/aria state is outside what these systems were built to see.
layout_awareness: None in any of the three, and in GROWN+UP's case this is an explicit design choice rather than an omission: the paper states its selected node features 'do not require rendering nor additional remote resources to obtain' -- i.e. the authors deliberately restricted themselves to statically-parseable DOM properties (no computed style, no bounding rects) specifically so the model would not need a rendering engine. Web2Text likewise parses raw (X)HTML via Jsoup with no rendering step. GoldMiner operates on crawled HTML directly. All three are therefore layout-blind in the same structural sense as this project's own fold, and for the same practical reason (avoiding the cost and fragility of a rendering dependency) rather than out of a privacy or determinism principle -- but the alignment with no_layout_in_the_fold is real regardless of motive. The GROWN+UP authors themselves flag this as a limitation to fix, not a virtue: their future-work section explicitly proposes adding 'visual features from the DOM such as the bounding rectangle and computed styles' as the next improvement, i.e. the paper's own authors see layout-blindness as leaving performance on the table, which is a useful data point about the tension this project accepts deliberately (no_layout_in_the_fold) and that this adjacent research treats as a temporary limitation to be removed.
javascript_required: No for any of the three, and again by explicit design for at least Web2Text and GROWN+UP: both parse raw static HTML markup with a DOM-tree library (Jsoup for Web2Text; unspecified but clearly static-parse for GROWN+UP given the no-rendering claim above) with no script execution. GoldMiner likewise processes crawled HTML text. This means all three, like the Reader-LM item, are downstream of whatever fetched the HTML and have no opinion about whether JS ran -- but unlike Reader-LM they were also EVALUATED exclusively on static-HTML-era corpora (CleanEval 2007, Dragnet 2012, CleanPortalEval undated but same era, 7-Web-Genre 2005, KI-04 2004), so there is no evidence in any of the three papers about how they behave on a JS-heavy composed-shadow-DOM page at all -- the static-HTML assumption is baked into training data as well as architecture.
evaluation_method: Three different metric families, which is itself a finding: this sub-literature has never converged on one evaluation protocol, echoing the fields.yaml's own observation that HTML-to-markdown comparisons are 'mutually contradictory'. Web2Text uses BLOCK-LEVEL classification metrics (accuracy, precision, recall, F1) where every DOM-leaf block is weighted equally regardless of length, evaluated with the CleanEval-standard Evert scoring script. GROWN+UP explicitly REJECTS block-classification accuracy as the metric (arguing 'it is possible to have a high accuracy on model-specific classification outputs but ultimately still have a low similarity between the extracted text and the actual ground truth') and instead adopts a TEXT-SIMILARITY metric borrowed from CETD: longest-common-subsequence (LCS) precision/recall/F1 over space-delimited word tokens between the full extracted text string and the full ground-truth text string, computed per page and macro-averaged -- a meaningfully different, arguably more end-to-end-honest measurement than Web2Text's block-accuracy approach, and the paper explicitly re-implements PRIOR systems (python-readability, python-goose, Dragnet, Web2Text, BoilerNet) on this same metric and the same dataset splits specifically to fix the apples-to-oranges problem it identifies in earlier work. GoldMiner uses the CleanEval-standard Levenshtein-edit-distance-based script (Evert's tool), reporting precision/recall/F-score plus a distinct DEDUPLICATION metric (percentage of unique sentences/characters in a crawled corpus) that is not directly comparable to either of the other two systems' numbers. None of the three evaluations is independent of its own authors (see evidence_independence and independent_oracle below), though GROWN+UP's re-implementation-on-common-splits effort is the strongest attempt at cross-system fairness found across any item in this set so far.
corpus_size_and_origins: Overlapping but not identical corpora across the three papers, and the overlaps expose real inconsistencies. CleanEval 2007: Web2Text reports an 'original split' of development (60 pages: divided into 55 train + 5 val) and test (676 pages), plus their OWN re-split of 531 train / 58 val / 148 test pages (needed because their 30,830-parameter model was judged too large for the original 55-page training set); GROWN+UP separately reports a CleanEval 'train/test split of 58/676' pages; GoldMiner reports a CleanEval TEST SET of 684 documents. Three papers, three slightly different page counts (676 vs 676 vs 684) for the same nominal dataset -- a small but real discrepancy worth flagging rather than silently reconciling, most plausibly explained by different exclusion of malformed/broken documents (GoldMiner's own paper notes CleanEval gold-standard files with broken words, e.g. '100-102.txt'). CleanEval's documents were built from English and Chinese Google search results for the terms 'picture, extents, raised, events' -- a narrow, keyword-seeded, 2007-era sampling method with no stated origin-domain count. Dragnet (used only by GROWN+UP among these three): pages from 2012, train/test split of 966/415, further split 869/97 for train/dev. CleanPortalEval (GoldMiner's own contribution): 70 pages from exactly 4 domains, deliberately small and deliberately domain-concentrated (multiple pages per domain) to test what CleanEval's 3-4-pages-per-domain structure cannot. GROWN+UP's SELF-SUPERVISED PRETRAINING corpus is separate again: 180,000 webpages sampled from the CommonCrawl 2008 archive, paired by matching URL subpaths for the same-website-prediction objective -- meaning the pretraining data (2008) is neither contemporaneous with CleanEval (2007, close) nor with Dragnet (2012, a 4-year gap) nor with the genre-classification datasets (7-Web 2005, KI-04 2004), a stylistic mismatch the authors acknowledge directly ('benchmark datasets from 2004 to 2012 which may differ stylistically from our pre-training corpus') while reporting that pretraining still helped. None of the three corpora used by any of these papers has origin-domain counts in the same range as this project's own 136-page/109-origin corpus, and none post-dates 2012 -- all evidence here is from a materially older web than the one the project's own fold is measured against.
reported_precision_recall: Full tables extracted from primary sources (PDF-to-text conversion of the arXiv/Polibits originals, not secondary summaries). WEB2TEXT (Table 1, block-level Acc./Precision/Recall/F1): on the original CleanEval split (train 55p, val 5p, test 676p) -- Web2Text 0.84 Acc / 0.88 P / 0.85 R / 0.86 F1; CRF baseline (Spousta et al., the prior CleanEval-competition-winning method) 0.82/0.87/0.81/0.84; BTE 0.79/0.79/0.89/0.83; boilerpipe default-ext 0.80/0.89/0.75/0.81; boilerpipe article-ext 0.72/0.91/0.59/0.71; boilerpipe largest-ext 0.60/0.93/0.36/0.52; Unfluff 0.71/0.90/0.57/0.70. On Web2Text's own larger re-split (train 531p, val 58p, test 148p): Web2Text improves to 0.86/0.87/0.90/0.88 F1, while every heuristic baseline's numbers on this harder 148-page test subset are reported LOWER than on the 676-page original test set (e.g. BTE drops to 0.75 Acc / 0.80 F1, boilerpipe default-ext collapses to 0.67 Acc / 0.64 F1) -- Web2Text's stated advantage over heuristics widens specifically on the split its own authors constructed, which is a methodological point worth flagging under evidence_independence. Retrieval extrinsic evaluation (Table 2, ClueWeb12): indexing Web2Text-cleaned text improved P@10/R@10/F1@10/MAP/nDCG over raw content and every baseline at significance level 0.05 across all four collection/model combinations tested (CW12-A and CW12-B, query-likelihood and relevance-model retrieval) -- e.g. CW12-A/QL: raw content nDCG 0.459 vs Web2Text 0.578, CRF 0.543. GROWN+UP (Table 2, Micro-F1%): upper bound 'perfect filter' CleanEval 97.9 / Dragnet 99.4 (not 100%, because some ground-truth text has no exact match in raw HTML -- an intrinsic ceiling, see fidelity note below); 'no filter' floor 89.8 / 64.9; python-readability 90.2/82.2; python-goose 82.9/76.1; CETD-DS 92.3/82.8; Dragnet(tool) 91.2+/-0.1 / 91.4+/-0.1; Web2Text (GROWN+UP's own re-implementation) 93.0+/-0.1 / 92.9+/-0.5; BoilerNet 92.7+/-0.1 / 93.8+/-0.3; GROWN+UP's headline L=5,T=5,F=256+pretrain model 93.4+/-0.2 / 96.9+/-0.3 (a closely related L=10,F=256+pretrain variant scores marginally higher on CleanEval at 93.5+/-0.1 but lacks Dragnet-comparable ablations reported at that setting). A footnoted caveat in the GROWN+UP paper itself: their re-run of Dragnet's own tool scores lower than Dragnet's original paper claimed, attributed to 'a different test set used and some additional clean-up of the ground truth text' -- i.e. even within one careful re-implementation effort, cross-paper numbers for the SAME tool disagree. GOLDMINER (Table II, CleanEval F-score/Precision/Recall): jusText+Onion 93.61/95.29/91.99; GoldMiner alone 93.24/95.51/91.08; GoldMiner+Onion 93.40/95.32/91.55; BoilerPipe 93.08/95.49/90.78; BTE 83.49/95.15/74.38 -- on CleanEval, GoldMiner does NOT outperform the simpler jusText+Onion baseline; the paper's own text concedes 'we do not get consistent improvement' here because CleanEval provides only 3-4 pages per domain, too few for GoldMiner's cross-page pattern-learning to exploit. Table III (CleanPortalEval, 70 pages/4 domains, GoldMiner's own purpose-built benchmark): GoldMiner+Onion 98.32/98.50/98.15 (best of the six systems compared), BoilerPipe 97.77/98.48/97.07, GoldMiner alone 91.16/86.48/96.38, jusText+Onion 87.26/78.82/97.72, BTE 90.68/92.91/88.56 -- here GoldMiner's advantage is clear, exactly as the paper predicts, because the benchmark was purpose-built to give GoldMiner's cross-page mechanism enough same-domain samples to work with. Table IV (three live Hungarian news portals, 2000 pages each, deduplication ratio not F-score): GoldMiner produced dramatically higher unique-sentence percentages than BTE and jusText (e.g. origo.hu: BTE 54% unique sentences / jusText 51% / GoldMiner 94%; index.hu: BTE 50% / jusText 71% / GoldMiner 91%), though the paper explicitly notes it has 'no estimate of how the different algorithms perform in terms of the amount/ratio of lost relevant content' on these three portals since they were not manually annotated -- the dedup win is real but its precision/recall cost is simply unmeasured for this specific table.
independent_oracle: Weak across all three, structurally similar to the Reader-LM item's weak-independent-oracle finding, but for a different reason: here the weakness is cross-paper metric incompatibility rather than shared-assumption contamination. Web2Text's own evaluation uses a standard external scoring script (Evert's CleanEval tool) rather than a self-defined metric, which is a point in its favor, but the comparison set (BTE, boilerpipe variants, Unfluff, and a CRF baseline the authors could not retrain and had to evaluate 'out of the box' on a different split) is assembled and run by Web2Text's own authors. GROWN+UP's explicit re-implementation-on-common-splits methodology is the closest thing to an oracle-like cross-check found in this file: by re-running Dragnet, Web2Text, BoilerNet, python-readability, python-goose, and CETD-DS all on the SAME train/test splits with the SAME LCS-based metric, the paper reduces (without eliminating) the risk that a reported win is an artifact of favorable-split selection -- but the re-implementation is still performed entirely by GROWN+UP's own authors, and the paper's own footnote about Dragnet's number disagreeing with Dragnet's original paper shows that even careful re-implementation is not the same as a third party's independent verification. GoldMiner's evaluation against jusText, BoilerPipe and BTE uses the same standard CleanEval script as Web2Text, which is again a real methodological plus, but GoldMiner is also the paper that INTRODUCES CleanPortalEval, the one benchmark on which it wins clearly -- authoring both the method and its most favorable evaluation corpus is the textbook shape of the evidence-independence problem this project's fields.yaml flags.
evidence_independence: All three are entirely author-produced, with no third-party benchmark located in this research that independently re-scores any of them (contrast the Reader-LM item, where the WCXB paper provided one genuinely independent, if secondary-sourced, contradicting data point). This is a materially weaker independent-evidence position than the Reader-LM item, not a stronger one, despite these systems' 2013-2022 academic pedigree feeling more rigorous than a vendor blog post -- academic peer review at ECIR/CIKM/Polibits checks methodology, not whether the authors' own numbers replicate elsewhere, and none of these three specific results was located being cited as a baseline in a later, differently-authored, large-scale benchmark such as WCXB (WCXB's own extractor list, per this project's other research, centers on rs-trafilatura and heuristic tools plus ReaderLM-v2 -- Web2Text, GROWN+UP and GoldMiner do not appear to be among WCXB's compared systems, [uncertain], based on what could be retrieved from that paper in this research). GROWN+UP's re-implementation effort is the strongest mitigation among the three but is still self-administered.
page_archetype_coverage: Not measured as a first-class dimension by any of the three -- none reports a per-archetype (article/forum/product/listing/documentation/service) breakdown in the WCXB sense. The closest analogues are narrower and structurally informative in their own right. GoldMiner's central finding IS an archetype-adjacent effect stated explicitly: performance depends on whether a page belongs to a domain with enough SAME-STRUCTURE siblings for cross-page pattern mining to work, which is a different axis from WCXB's per-type spread but points at the same underlying truth WCXB documents -- extraction difficulty is not uniform across page populations, and a single aggregate score hides which population a system actually handles well. GROWN+UP's genre-classification benchmark (7-Web, KI-04) is adjacent to archetype awareness but measures a different task (classifying a whole page's genre, not per-archetype extraction fidelity) and its own paper notes the genre-classification field's own datasets are 'extremely diverse' with 'the vast majority proprietary,' i.e. even that adjacent literature lacks a standard archetype-labeled corpus. No system here was tested on anything resembling WCXB's seven structural types.
script_and_locale_behaviour: Thin evidence across all three, and what exists suggests these systems are more script-fragile than the trafilatura-class heuristics elsewhere in this project's item list, not less. CleanEval's corpus (used by Web2Text and GoldMiner) includes both English AND Chinese pages by original design, but neither paper reports a script-disaggregated score -- performance is reported as one pooled number across both scripts. Web2Text's 128 block features include several that are inherently script-sensitive by construction: average word length, sentence-length statistics via punctuation-based sentence splitting, 'ratio of words with capital [letter]' (meaningless for scripts without case, e.g. Chinese, Japanese, Thai, Arabic), and a stopword-ratio feature keyed to an unspecified (presumably English-only or per-language) stopword list -- none of this is discussed as a limitation in the paper, but the feature list itself is evidence that the model's inputs assume Latin-script, whitespace-segmented, cased text as the default case, with CJK content likely degrading multiple features simultaneously rather than gracefully. GROWN+UP's use of Universal Sentence Encoder (USE) embeddings for text/class/id is explicitly described as 'cross-lingual,' which is a genuine mitigation not present in Web2Text -- USE was trained multilingually and does not depend on whitespace segmentation or case -- but no per-script ablation is reported to confirm this holds in practice for the model as a whole. GoldMiner/jusText's stopword-and-link-density approach inherits jusText's own documented language-dependent function-word list requirement, meaning GoldMiner is only as multilingual as whatever jusText language pack is configured, with no discussion of non-Latin scripts in the paper (its own worked examples are Hungarian and English). None of the three offers RTL or whitespace-free-segmentation-specific evidence.
leaks_outward: None for any of the three -- all are in-process algorithms operating on already-fetched HTML/text with no network calls of their own, structurally identical to every other in-process item in this project's list. GoldMiner's per-domain learning phase does require crawling ~100 sample pages from a domain before it can trim subsequent pages from that domain, which is a property of the CRAWLER using GoldMiner, not of GoldMiner itself, but is worth flagging as an operational implication: adopting GoldMiner's mechanism means committing to a warm-up crawl per origin before extraction quality improves, a cost this project's own single-page-oriented fold does not currently pay.
mechanism_detectability: Zero for all three, same reasoning as every other pure post-processing/analysis item in this set: none of them touches the live page, executes in the page's JS context, or is observable by the origin. This is a point of total alignment with the project's stealth requirements and, unlike layout-blindness, is not something any of the three authors treat as a limitation to fix -- it simply never arises as a concern in any of the three papers because none was designed with an adversarial page in mind.
countermeasures: Not applicable in the adversarial-detection sense (no adversary to counter, per mechanism_detectability). The nearest analogous concept is ROBUSTNESS TO DOMAIN VARIETY, which the three handle very differently: Web2Text and GROWN+UP rely on the generalization properties of their trained weights, with no explicit defensive mechanism against out-of-distribution pages beyond whatever the training corpus's diversity provides; GoldMiner's per-domain learning phase is itself a built-in adaptation mechanism (it re-learns a boundary pattern for every new domain rather than relying on one global model), which is arguably a stronger form of robustness to unseen page structures than either neural model offers, at the cost of needing repeated same-domain samples.
measured_fidelity_cost: Not a hardening tradeoff in the project's privacy sense for any of the three (no privacy hardening is being traded against fidelity here). The closest measured tradeoff in this file is GoldMiner's Onion-post-filtering interaction: applying Onion (near-duplicate paragraph removal) after GoldMiner or jusText measurably TRADES coherence for deduplication -- Onion increases precision but decreases recall on CleanEval (Table II: jusText 93.61 F1 alone vs the paper's implicit unfiltered jusText being higher on recall), and the paper gives a concrete worked example (CleanEval file 127.txt, 'An open letter to KPLU') where Onion strips a salutation sentence because it recurs as a template greeting elsewhere in the corpus, leaving grammatically truncated output -- a directly measured, named cost of a specific hardening step, which is exactly the kind of number this project's own measured_fidelity_cost field is trying to capture, just from an adjacent literature rather than this project's own privacy hardening.
gate_state_at_capture: Not represented or discussed in any of the three papers -- all predate or are contemporaneous with, but do not engage with, the consent-banner-prevalence literature this project's fields.yaml cites. As with Reader-LM and the Patricia-trie item, gate state is a property of the capture pipeline that none of these extraction-stage systems has any visibility into.
determinism: Deterministic at inference for Web2Text and GROWN+UP given fixed trained weights -- both are feed-forward classification pipelines (CNN+Viterbi; GNN+classifier head) with no sampling step at prediction time, a sharp and favorable contrast with Reader-LM's default non-deterministic decoding. GoldMiner is deterministic within a fixed learned per-domain pattern, but the LEARNING phase itself has an order-dependence risk worth naming: the paper describes selecting 'the most frequent uniquely identifiable pattern' from a sample of ~100 pages, which is deterministic given a fixed sample but will select a DIFFERENT boundary pattern if the sample of 100 pages changes (different crawl order, different day, site redesign mid-sample) -- so GoldMiner's per-domain determinism is conditional on a frozen sample in a way the other two are not.
determinism_across_versions: Not directly discussed in any paper, but inferable from architecture. Web2Text and GROWN+UP's output depends on the specific trained weight checkpoint published; using a different training run (even with identical hyperparameters, given both use stochastic optimization -- GROWN+UP's own Table 2 reports standard deviations across repeated runs, e.g. +/-0.1 to +/-0.7 F1 points, meaning retraining from scratch measurably changes the model) will shift output, and neither paper publishes a stability bound across independent training runs beyond the ablation table's own reported variance. GoldMiner's cross-version risk is different in kind: it depends on jusText's own version/language-pack behavior plus whatever DOM parser is used to find the 'nearest common parent' tag, so a change in either dependency could silently shift which tag pattern is learned for a given domain, with no versioning discipline discussed in the paper.
reproducibility: Mixed. Both Web2Text and GROWN+UP publish source code (MIT and Apache-2.0 respectively) including, in GROWN+UP's case, the benchmarking implementation itself -- a genuine plus for reproducibility relative to Reader-LM's undocumented training corpus. However, GROWN+UP's pretraining corpus (180K CommonCrawl-2008-derived pages) is not stated to be published as a frozen artifact, so pretraining from scratch is not exactly reproducible even with the code, only fine-tuning from the authors' published checkpoint is. Web2Text's automatic block-labeling procedure (recovering block-level labels from page/clean-text pairs via a divide-and-conquer unique-substring-matching and dynamic-programming alignment, with a 2/3-of-text-aligned threshold for partial matches) is itself a heuristic pipeline with a stated approximation threshold, meaning the TRAINING LABELS are algorithmically reconstructed and could in principle differ slightly between reimplementations even from the same source corpus. GoldMiner's results explicitly depend on CleanPortalEval, which the paper states is 'open to the public' on GitHub (ppke-nlpg/CleanPortalEval, confirmed to exist during this research), and separately links a results-download repository (ppke-nlpg/boilerplateResults) -- both artifacts being public and specifically named is a genuine reproducibility strength for GoldMiner's own headline result.
failure_modes: Distinct per system and instructive by contrast with Reader-LM's confabulation. Web2Text: the paper names exactly one architecture-level risk -- a hyperlink inside a text paragraph could in principle receive a different label than its surrounding text (a boundary-alignment artifact of DOM-leaf-level block segmentation) -- but reports that empirical evaluation found NO such cases in practice; beyond this, failure is purely a classification-accuracy question (the F1 gap from 1.0), not a distinct qualitative failure category. GROWN+UP: the paper's own honesty about an intrinsic ceiling is the most useful failure-mode finding in this file -- even a 'perfect' boilerplate filter cannot reach 100% F1 (97.9% CleanEval / 99.4% Dragnet) because SOME ground-truth text has no exact correspondence in the raw HTML at all, meaning a nontrivial fraction of any boilerplate-removal benchmark's headroom is an artifact of annotation/alignment noise rather than model capability -- any F1 number in this space should be read against that ceiling, not against 100%. GoldMiner: two named failure modes, both structural rather than incidental. (1) INSUFFICIENT SAME-DOMAIN SAMPLES -- on CleanEval's 3-4-pages-per-domain structure, GoldMiner 'has no chance to learn anything relevant about the structure' and produces no consistent improvement over the jusText baseline it wraps; this is a hard applicability boundary, not a tunable weakness. (2) ONION POST-FILTERING INCOHERENCE -- the near-duplicate-paragraph removal step commonly used alongside GoldMiner strips repeated sentences from the MIDDLE of otherwise-unique paragraphs when those specific sentences happen to be template boilerplate (the 'Good Morning!' / salutation-stripping example), producing grammatically fragmented 'torso' text -- a distinct and directly observed degradation mode this project's own fold-plus-dedup design should watch for if it ever layers a similar cross-page near-duplicate filter on top of extraction.
failure_visibility: Loud/measurable for all three, a genuinely favorable contrast with Reader-LM. Because none of the three generates content, their failures are entirely of the 'wrong label on existing, inspectable text' kind: a block that should have been kept was discarded (a recall miss, visibly absent from output) or a block that should have been discarded was kept (a precision miss, visibly present and traceable to a specific DOM node/text span). Both kinds of error are auditable by diffing extractor output against the source HTML -- there is no equivalent of Reader-LM's plausible-looking fabricated biography, because there is no generation step that could produce ungrounded content. This is the primary safety argument in favor of a classifier-based approach over a generative one for any pipeline stage that must fail loudly, though it does not make classifier-based extraction compatible with this project's structure_agnosticism constraint (see constraint_violation_ledger).
scale_limits: Two genuinely reported numbers. Web2Text: 54ms per web page on average on a 2.8GHz Intel Core i5 Macbook (35ms DOM parsing + feature extraction, 19ms neural forward pass + Viterbi decoding) -- this is squarely in the same performance class as the heuristic extractors elsewhere in this project's item list (compare rs-trafilatura's cited ~44ms/page) and is ORDERS OF MAGNITUDE faster than Reader-LM's GPU-bound multi-second-per-page generation, because Web2Text's CNNs are small (30,830 total parameters across both networks) and run once per page rather than autoregressively token-by-token. GROWN+UP's own model sizes are reported (11.5M parameters for its headline L=5,T=5,F=256 variant) but no per-page latency figure was found in the extracted text of the paper -- [uncertain] on GROWN+UP's throughput; given it is a multi-layer GNN with Transformer blocks operating on the full page graph plus 512-dimensional USE sentence embeddings computed per text/class/id field, it is very unlikely to match Web2Text's sub-100ms figure, but this is an inference from architecture, not a measured number. GoldMiner's own per-page cost is not separately reported (it is dominated by jusText's cost, described elsewhere in this project's items as fast, plus a one-time per-domain learning cost amortized over however many pages are subsequently crawled from that domain -- the amortization curve itself is not characterized).
delta_cost_model: None defined by any of the three, and none is meaningfully definable without architectural change, though for a different reason than Reader-LM. Web2Text and GROWN+UP process each page independently and in full on every call -- there is no notion of re-classifying only the DOM nodes that changed since a prior extraction, so a single DOM mutation costs a full-page re-run of the CNN/GNN forward pass, same structural mismatch with o_delta as Reader-LM, just cheaper in absolute terms (milliseconds vs seconds). GoldMiner is the interesting partial exception: its EXPENSIVE step (the ~100-page domain-learning phase) is amortized across many subsequent pages from the same domain and does not need to be repeated per page or per delta -- once a domain's boundary pattern is learned, applying it to a new or changed page is a cheap tag-boundary lookup plus a jusText pass, which is closer in spirit to the project's own preference for expensive-work-once, cheap-work-per-change than either neural model offers. This makes GoldMiner's TWO-PHASE structure (learn once per domain, apply cheaply per page) the one architectural idea in this file that is not simply incompatible with o_delta by construction.
reanchoring_stability: Not addressed by any of the three as a named concept -- none proposes or measures a mechanism for tracking whether a specific piece of content is 'the same' content across a DOM mutation or a re-crawl, because all three treat each page as a fresh, independent classification problem rather than as a mutable object needing content continuity. GoldMiner's per-domain boundary PATTERN is the closest analogue to something re-anchorable across pages of a site (the same tag-pattern boundary is expected to keep matching as new pages from a domain are crawled), but the paper gives no measured rate of pattern drift as sites redesign, and by its own account the boundary pattern must be re-learned whenever the sample no longer reflects the domain's current structure -- there is no incremental or automatic re-anchoring, only full re-learning.
adversarial_exposure: Not evaluated by any of the three, and the structural picture differs meaningfully from Reader-LM's. Because Web2Text and GROWN+UP are classifiers over EXISTING DOM content rather than generators, they cannot be manipulated into fabricating attacker-chosen output the way a page containing injected natural-language instructions could plausibly steer an autoregressive Reader-LM (see that item's adversarial_exposure field) -- there is no next-token-prediction mechanism here for an instruction embedded in the page to hijack. The residual risk is narrower and more conventional: a classifier can be FOOLED into mislabeling attacker-crafted content as main-content (e.g. text styled/positioned/tagged to mimic the statistical signature of an article body, a known general adversarial-example risk for any text/feature classifier), but none of the three papers tests this, and none of the three reads layout any more than the project's own fold does, so none can distinguish rendered from concealed content any better than a purely deterministic approach could. GoldMiner's per-domain pattern-learning has its own distinct exposure: an adversarial or malformed sample page injected into the ~100-page learning sample could skew which tag boundary is learned as 'the' article pattern for that domain, a data-poisoning-shaped risk specific to its two-phase design that neither of the other two systems has (since they use fixed, pre-trained weights rather than learning per-target-domain).
provenance_carrying: None in any of the three, structurally identical to Reader-LM on this specific field despite the very different generation-vs-classification mechanism: all three emit plain extracted text (or, for GROWN+UP, per-node classification labels that a caller must separately map back to source positions) with no built-in address, xpath, or capture-time token traveling with the output by default. GROWN+UP's per-node classification output is, in principle, more amenable to provenance-carrying than Web2Text's or GoldMiner's flat text output, since each classified unit already corresponds to a specific graph node with an implicit position in the original DOM -- but the paper's stated output is the classification LABEL per node, not a provenance-tagged export, so carrying that link forward into a downstream artifact would be an integration choice made by whoever deploys the model, not a property the paper delivers.
roundtrip_safety: Not applicable/not evaluated for any of the three in the serialize-parse-serialize sense this project's other items use -- none of the three defines an inverse operation (there is no 'reconstruct the original HTML from the extracted text' direction), and all three are LOSSY BY DESIGN (that is the entire point of boilerplate removal), so a fixed-point round-trip test is not a meaningful check for this category of tool the way it is for a serializer like the trie or even, more weakly, for Reader-LM's HTML-to-Markdown direction.
token_budget_and_ordering: Not addressed by any of the three as a first-class concern -- all predate the LLM-context-budget framing this field is written for, and none was designed with a downstream token-limited consumer in mind. The nearest relevant property is that all three PRESERVE DOCUMENT ORDER by construction (Web2Text's block sequence follows source-code order; GROWN+UP's per-node labels can be walked back into DOM order; GoldMiner's cropped region is a contiguous HTML span), so a caller wanting ordered output gets it 'for free' as a side effect of how each system is built, the same default-document-order property noted for the Patricia trie and contrasted there with Reader-LM's lack of guaranteed structural completeness -- but none offers a budget-aware truncation or prioritization mechanism of any kind.
representation_cost: Cheap for Web2Text (see scale_limits: 54ms/page, 30,830 total model parameters, no GPU required per the reported Macbook CPU benchmark), unmeasured but architecturally heavier for GROWN+UP (11.5M parameters for the benchmarked variant, plus a 512-dimensional Universal Sentence Encoder forward pass per text/class/id field per node, which is itself a nontrivial embedding-model cost layered on top of the GNN, though still far short of an autoregressive LLM's cost profile), and effectively free per page for GoldMiner after the one-time per-domain learning cost (a jusText pass plus a lookup against an already-learned tag-boundary pattern). None reports tokens-per-page or output-size-versus-input-size ratios, since none targets a token-budgeted consumer (see token_budget_and_ordering); the relevant cost dimension for all three is compute-per-page, not representation-size.
what_could_be_adopted: One clear mechanism, sourced from GoldMiner rather than either neural model. GOLDMINER'S CROSS-PAGE UNIQUENESS SIGNAL -- flag a paragraph/subtree as boilerplate if it recurs verbatim (or near-verbatim) across a sample of other pages from the same origin, and treat the nearest common ancestor of the surviving unique content as a candidate content boundary -- is a DETERMINISTIC, STATISTICAL, fully auditable procedure with no gradient training and no black-box weights: it is closer in kind to MinHash/SimHash-style recurrence detection (already a first-class item elsewhere in this project's list) than to a neural classifier, and it could in principle be reformulated as a structure-agnostic, per-origin cross-page frequency count layered on top of the project's own deterministic fold rather than replacing it -- exactly the kind of actuator-layer signal (this content is common-to-N-siblings, therefore likely templated) that a downstream consumer could use without the fold itself ever making a content/boilerplate judgment call. This is a genuinely different category of finding from the Reader-LM item's TER-metric suggestion: GoldMiner offers a MECHANISM worth taking, not merely a metric worth borrowing. Nothing from Web2Text or GROWN+UP proper is adoptable in the fold: both are exactly the kind of trained classifier 'naming a region' that structure_agnosticism explicitly forbids, and their value here is calibrational, not architectural -- their published F1 numbers (Web2Text 0.86-0.88, GROWN+UP 93-97% Micro-F1 depending on corpus) are useful EXTERNAL REFERENCE POINTS for how good a maximally-informed, fully-supervised, corpus-specific classifier can get at this task, against which the project's own deterministic fold's recall/precision (85.5%/98.3% per the project's own open_questions) can be sanity-checked as a ceiling comparison, without adopting the classifiers themselves.
constraint_violation_ledger: structure_agnosticism -- WEB2TEXT: REJECTED. It is, definitionally, a trained classifier that labels every DOM leaf as content-region or not, which is precisely the 'classifier naming a region' the constraint prohibits, regardless of how well it performs. GROWN+UP: REJECTED for the same reason, more so -- its node features explicitly encode class/id attribute SEMANTICS via sentence embeddings (a step closer to 'reading the page author's own naming conventions as a content signal' than Web2Text's purely structural/lexical features), which is a heavier violation of the letter of the constraint even though it is learned rather than hand-authored. GOLDMINER: REJECTED AS PUBLISHED (it still ends in a rule-based classifier, jusText, making the final good/bad call region-by-region) but its CROSS-PAGE UNIQUENESS-COUNTING MECHANISM specifically is ADOPTABLE IN THE ACTUATOR LAYER ONLY, since a frequency count is not a semantic label and could be exposed as a signal for a downstream consumer to use, not as a decision the fold itself makes. no_layout_in_the_fold -- ADOPTABLE AS-IS for all three on the narrow point that none reads geometry (GROWN+UP explicitly by design), though as with Reader-LM this is a coincidental convenience-driven alignment in two of the three cases (Web2Text, GoldMiner), not a considered privacy/determinism stance, and GROWN+UP's own authors state layout-blindness as a limitation they intend to remove in future work, which cuts against reading this alignment as evidence the wider field endorses the project's position. o_delta -- REJECTED for Web2Text and GROWN+UP (full-page re-inference on every call, no incremental cost model, same structural mismatch as Reader-LM though far cheaper in absolute wall-clock terms). GoldMiner is the PARTIAL EXCEPTION noted under delta_cost_model: its two-phase learn-once/apply-cheaply structure is directionally compatible with amortized-cost thinking even though the paper never frames it in o_delta terms and it still requires a full domain-level batch (not a true per-change delta) to refresh. no_mocks -- NOT DIRECTLY APPLICABLE as a compliance question for any of the three (none is a stub; all are real, if dated, systems), but as with Reader-LM, any live deployment of Web2Text or GROWN+UP would need continuous regression testing against real pages rather than unit-testable deterministic assertions, because both depend on trained weights whose behavior on novel inputs is not analytically guaranteed -- GoldMiner is the exception here too, being fully inspectable/traceable (its 'decision' is a specific learned tag-pattern that can be printed and audited directly). closed_shadow_roots_stay_closed -- NOT APPLICABLE for any of the three; none has any relationship to shadow DOM access, all operating purely on whatever serialized/parsed HTML they are handed. OVERALL VERDICT -- Web2Text and GROWN+UP: NEGATIVE ORACLE ONLY for the fold role (their SOTA numbers are useful as an external ceiling/calibration reference for the project's own recall metric, and Web2Text's low-latency, non-generative, loud-failure design is a genuinely instructive contrast case against Reader-LM's expensive, generative, silent-failure design even though neither is adoptable directly). GoldMiner: the one item across BOTH files in this research pass with a plausible, narrowly-scoped ADOPTABLE-IN-THE-ACTUATOR-LAYER mechanism (cross-page content-uniqueness counting), distinct from being adoptable as a whole system.
governance_signal_handling: Not addressed by any of the three -- all predate or ignore the robots.txt/Content-Signals/ai.txt/AIPREF vocabulary this field asks about, consistent with their era and their focus on content classification rather than crawl policy. GoldMiner's domain-level sampling phase (crawling ~100 pages from a domain before extraction quality improves) is the one point in this file with an operational governance interaction worth flagging: a domain-learning crawl of that shape is exactly the kind of behavior a Content-Signals or robots.txt policy might want to gate or rate-limit differently from ordinary single-page fetches, but none of the three papers engages with this at all.
legal_basis_and_pii_posture: Not addressed by any of the three papers, and the structural picture here is more benign than Reader-LM's: because none of the three is generative, none carries Reader-LM's distinct risk of FABRICATING plausible-looking personal data that could be mistaken for scraped fact -- whatever PII these systems retain or discard is PII that was genuinely present in the source page, the same category of concern as any other extractor in this project's item list, not a novel category. GoldMiner's per-domain sample retention (the ~100 pages used to learn a boundary pattern) is a specific, nameable data-retention question -- are those sample pages kept, and for how long, after the pattern is learned -- that the paper does not address and that any adopting implementation would need to decide explicitly.
